plants.ecological_importance: Its long-lasting yellow flowers are an important nectar source for bees and butterflies, and its seed pods provide food for birds and mammals. It is the state flower of Kerala and commonly used as a shade and avenue tree on Indian campuses.
threats: Over-harvesting of bark and pods for traditional medicine in some regions
conservation_actions: Plant as a native avenue/shade tree instead of exotic ornamentals
Avoid unnecessary bark stripping when harvesting for medicinal use
Protect existing mature specimens on campus and roadside plantings
plants.description: A medium-sized deciduous tree known for its cascading clusters of bright yellow flowers that bloom in early summer, giving it the common name 'Golden Shower Tree'.

plants.ecological_importance: Provides year-round shade and dense canopy that supports birds and insects, and its flowers are a nectar source for pollinators. Widely valued in traditional medicine and organic pest control, reducing reliance on synthetic pesticides.
threats: Being displaced by fast-growing exotic ornamental species in urban landscaping
Soil compaction and root damage from construction near mature trees
conservation_actions: Prioritize neem over exotic species in campus and urban afforestation drives
Protect root zones of mature trees during construction
Encourage use of neem-based biopesticides over chemical alternatives
plants.description: A fast-growing evergreen tree with bitter-tasting leaves and small white flowers, one of the most widely used medicinal and pesticidal plants in South Asia.

plants.ecological_importance: A keystone species in many Indian ecosystems: its figs provide food for numerous bird and bat species almost year-round, and it releases oxygen at a high rate, contributing significantly to local air quality.
threats: Urban development removing large old-growth specimens
Restricted root growth from pavement and concrete around campus/urban plantings
conservation_actions: Preserve mature peepal trees during campus and city planning
Leave adequate unpaved soil area around the base for root growth
Plant saplings in open ground rather than confined urban planters
plants.description: A large, long-living fig tree with distinctive heart-shaped leaves that taper to a long drip tip, considered sacred in several Indian religious traditions.

plants.ecological_importance: One of the most ecologically significant trees in India; its extensive canopy and aerial prop roots create microhabitats for birds, insects, and epiphytes, and its figs are a critical food source for many species. It is the National Tree of India.
threats: Loss of open space needed for its wide-spreading canopy and prop roots
Removal of old-growth individuals during urban and campus construction
conservation_actions: Designate mature banyan trees as protected campus/heritage trees
Allow sufficient open ground for aerial root establishment
Include banyan in native-species afforestation and campus greening plans
plants.description: A massive, long-lived fig tree that spreads outward via aerial prop roots which thicken into secondary trunks, allowing a single tree to cover a very large area over centuries.

plants.ecological_importance: Provides nectar-rich orange-red flower clusters that support pollinating insects, and its dense evergreen canopy offers year-round shelter for birds. It holds strong cultural and religious significance in South Asia.
threats: Overharvesting of bark for traditional/Ayurvedic medicine, which can kill the tree
Habitat loss and deforestation reducing wild populations
Slow natural regeneration in the wild
conservation_actions: Source Ashoka bark/products only from certified sustainable cultivation, not wild-harvested trees
Support nursery propagation and campus/community planting programs
Protect and monitor existing wild and planted populations
plants.description: A small evergreen tree with fragrant orange-to-red flower clusters, historically and culturally revered across the Indian subcontinent, now considered vulnerable in the wild.

plants.ecological_importance: Its flowers support a wide range of pollinating insects, and its fruit is an important food source for birds, bats, and mammals. Mango trees also provide dense, long-lasting shade and are a dominant part of many Indian campus and orchard landscapes.
threats: Monoculture orchard practices reducing genetic diversity of wild/local varieties
Loss of older heritage trees to land-use change
conservation_actions: Preserve local and heritage mango cultivars alongside commercial varieties
Retain mature mango trees in campus green spaces
Support pollinator-friendly practices (avoid excess pesticide use during flowering)
plants.description: A large evergreen tree, the source of the mango fruit and the national fruit of India, widely cultivated across South Asia for millennia.

plants.ecological_importance: Its aromatic flowers attract pollinators and its fruit is eaten and dispersed by wildlife. The tree is also considered sacred and is frequently planted near temples and campuses, helping maintain green cover in urban areas.
plants.conservation_status: Near Threatened in wild populations (though common in cultivation)
threats: Declining regeneration outside cultivated and temple/campus plantings
conservation_actions: Encourage planting in campus and community green spaces
Protect naturally occurring wild individuals where found
Use seeds from local trees for afforestation rather than only relying on cultivated stock
plants.description: A slow-growing, spiny deciduous tree bearing hard-shelled aromatic fruit, long used in traditional medicine and considered sacred in Hindu tradition.

plants.ecological_importance: Its small white flowers attract bees and other pollinators, and its berries are eaten by birds. As a common understorey shrub/small tree, it contributes to layered vegetation structure in campus and garden landscapes.
threats: Overharvesting of leaves in cultivated settings can stress individual plants
Loss of understorey habitat due to urban landscaping that favors lawns over shrub layers
conservation_actions: Maintain shrub-layer plantings on campus rather than clearing to bare lawn
Practice moderate, sustainable leaf harvesting
Include in native-species landscaping and pollinator gardens
plants.description: A small aromatic tree/shrub whose leaves are a staple flavoring herb across South Asian cuisine, and whose small berries provide food for local bird species.
